{{Short description|Extinct Aramaic language of Turkey and Syria}} {{Hatnote|Not to be confused with the [[Turoyo language]], also called Suryoyo.}} {{Infobox language | name = Mlaḥso | nativename = {{lang|lhs|ܡܠܰܚܣܳܐ}} {{tlit|lhs|Mlaḥsô}}
{{lang|lhs|ܣܘܪܝܝܐ}} {{tlit|lha|Suryô}} | states = [[Turkey]], [[Syria]] | region = Originally two villages ([[Yünlüce, Lice|Mlaḥsô]] and ˁAnşa) near [[Lice, Turkey|Lice]] in [[Diyarbakır Province]] of southeastern [[Turkey]], later also [[Qamishli]] in northeastern [[Syria]]. | speakers = | extinct = 1999 | ref = e17 | familycolor = Afro-Asiatic | fam2 = [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] | fam3 = [[Central Semitic languages|Central Semitic]] | fam4 = [[Northwest Semitic languages|Northwest Semitic]] | fam5 = [[Aramaic language|Aramaic]] | fam6 = [[Eastern Aramaic languages|Eastern Aramaic]] | fam7 = [[Central Neo-Aramaic]] | iso3 = lhs | glotto = mlah1239 | glottorefname = Mlahso | altname = Suryoyo, Surayt }} {{Assyrian culture}} '''Mlaḥsô''' or '''Mlahso''' ({{langx|syc|ܡܠܰܚܣܳܐ}}), sometimes referred to as '''Suryoyo''' or '''Surayt''', is an extinct or dormant [[Central Neo-Aramaic|Central Neo-Aramaic language]]. It was traditionally spoken in eastern [[Turkey]] and later also in northeastern [[Syria]] by ethnically [[Assyrian people|Assyrian]] [[Syriac Orthodox Christians]].[https://academic.oup.com/jss/article-abstract/XXX/2/265/1633853?redirectedFrom=fulltext&login=false {{cite journal|last=Jastrow|first=Otto|title=Mlaḥsô: An Unknown Neo-Aramaic Language of Turkey|journal=Journal of Semitic Studies|date=1985|volume=30|issue=2|pages=265–270|doi=}}]. The Mlaḥsô language (Surayt of Mlaḥsô) is closely related to the [[Turoyo language|Surayt of Turabdin]] but sufficiently different to be considered a separate language, with the syntax of the language having retained more features of [[Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] than Turoyo.{{Cite news|url=https://www.ethnologue.com/language/lhs|title=Mlahsö|work=Ethnologue|access-date=2017-05-14}} It was spoken in the villages of [[Yünlüce, Lice|Mlaḥsô]] ({{langx|tr|Yünlüce}}, {{langx|ku|Mela}}), a village established by two monks from the [[Tur Abdin]] mountain range, and in the village of ˁAnşa near [[Lice, Turkey|Lice]], [[Diyarbakır]], [[Turkey]]. ==Etymology== The name of the village and the language is derived from the earlier Aramaic word ''mālaḥtā'', 'salt marsh'. The literary Syriac name for the language is ''Mlaḥthoyo''. The native speakers of Mlaḥsô referred to their language simply as ''Suryô'', or Syriac.Jastrow, Otto. 1997. "Der Neuaramaische Dialek von Mlahso." In British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies, reviewed by Geoffrey Khan. 299-300. British Society for Middle Eastern Studies. ==History and distribution== According to the oral tradition of the people of Mlaḥsô, their village was founded several centuries ago by two brothers from [[Midyat]]. The tradition recounts that the brothers had a dream in which they were instructed to leave Midyat and build a church at a location that would be revealed to them. Following this vision, they eventually arrived in Mlaḥsô and constructed the church of Mar Smuni. This church remained in existence for centuries until 1915–1916, when most of the inhabitants of Mlaḥsô were massacred during the events of that period.Jastrow 1978 (cited in n. 1 above), p. 34. Linguistic evidence supports the notion that the Mlaḥsô language and [[Turoyo language|Turoyo]] were once part of a common linguistic unit before diverging into distinct languages. This suggests that while both languages share a common origin, they must have separated several centuries ago, each developing along an independent trajectory.Hans Jürgen Polotsky, "Zakho," in Franz Rosenthal (ed.), ''An Aramaic Handbook'', Part II.1 (Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 1967), p. 13ff. The language was still spoken by a handful of people in the 1970s. The [[Last speaker of language|last fluent native speaker]] of Mlaḥsô, Ibrahim Ḥanna, died in 1999 in [[Qamishli]].{{cite web|url=https://www.usek.edu.lb/Content/Files/CSR/RCMME/20140801RCMMENeoAramaic.pdf|title=The Neo-Aramaic Languages|quote=Ibrahim Ḥanna was the last speaker of the Mlaḥso language, as the village was destroyed in 1915 during the Armenian genocide. He died in 1999 in Qāmišli in Syria|access-date=2024-06-01}} His daughters, Munira in [[Qamishli]], Shamiram in Lebanon, and son Dr. Isḥaq Ibrahim in Germany are the only speakers left with some limited native proficiency of the language. Recordings of Ibrahim Ḥanna speaking the language are available on [http://www.semarch.uni-hd.de/tondokumente.php43?LD_ID=4&RG_ID=9&ORT_ID=12&lang=en Heidelberg University's Semitic Sound Archive] which were done by Otto Jastrow, a prominent German semiticist who is credited as the modern "discoverer" of the language and published the first modern research papers on the existence of Mlaḥsô and its linguistic features. On 3 May 2009, a historical event in the history of the Mlaḥsô Surayt language took place. The [[Suroyo TV]] television station aired the program series ''[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uswfjcVLHBg Dore w yawmotho]'', which was about the village Mlaḥsô (and the Tur Abdin village Tamarze). Dr. Isḥaq Ibrahim, the son of Ibrahim Ḥanna, was a guest and spoke in the Mlaḥsô language with his sisters Shamiram in Lebanon and Munira in [[Qamishli]] live on the phone. Otto Jastrow was also interviewed regarding his expertise on Mlaḥsô. [[Assyrian people|Assyrians]] from Tur Abdin and those present at the show were able to hear the language spoken live for the first time at the event. The extinction of Mlaḥsô can be attributed to the small amount of original speakers of the language, and them being limited to two isolated villages, resulting in a disproportionate loss of speakers during the [[Assyrian genocide]] compared to Turoyo and other variants of Neo-Aramaic. ==Phonology== Mlahsô is phonologically less conservative than Turoyo. This is particularly noticeable in the use of ''s'' and ''z'' for classical ''θ'' and ''ð''. The classical ''v'' has been retained though, while it has collapsed into ''w'' in Turoyo. Also sometimes ''y'' ([[International Phonetic Alphabet|IPA]] /j/) replaces ''ġ''.
